questiontext.text: Why is validation needed in the Product class (e.g. Shop 2.2) and in general?

answer.text: To prevent impossible or nonsensical values being stored in the object.

feedback.text: Correct — validation protects object integrity.

answer.text: To make the constructor run faster.

feedback.text: No — speed is not the goal here.

answer.text: Because Java requires validation for all classes.

feedback.text: Incorrect — Java doesn’t enforce validation; programmers must.

answer.text: So that getters do not need to return values.

feedback.text: No — getters always return values; validation is unrelated.

questiontext.text: When a numeric field fails validation in the constructor, what should happen?

answer.text: The field is set to a fixed default value.

feedback.text: Exactly — e.g., invalid productCode becomes 9999.

answer.text: The program stops with an error.

feedback.text: No — validation avoids errors, it doesn’t cause them.

answer.text: The field is left uninitialised.

feedback.text: Incorrect — Java won’t leave fields floating in the void.

answer.text: The user is asked to re-enter the data automatically.

feedback.text: No — constructors don’t normally loop back to the user.

questiontext.text: How is invalid String input typically handled in the constructor?

answer.text: The String is truncated to the permitted maximum length.

feedback.text: Correct — Strings use truncation rather than a fixed default.

answer.text: It becomes “INVALID”.

feedback.text: No — there’s no dramatic renaming.

answer.text: The field is assigned null.

feedback.text: Incorrect — null would cause more problems.

answer.text: The program automatically shortens it using setUnitCost().

feedback.text: No — unit cost has nothing to do with names!

answer.text: Values at, just inside, and just outside the allowed limits.

feedback.text: Right — boundaries define the edges of valid input.

answer.text: Random values only.

feedback.text: No — boundaries are deliberate, not random.

answer.text: Only invalid values.

feedback.text: No — valid and invalid cases are needed.

answer.text: Only the default values.

feedback.text: No — defaults are part of testing but not the whole thing.

questiontext.text: What is the role of a Loop Control Variable (LCV)?

answer.text: It determines whether the loop continues or stops.

feedback.text: Correct — the LCV is central to loop behaviour.

answer.text: It prints data to the console.

feedback.text: No — printing is not its job.

answer.text: It stores all input values.

feedback.text: Incorrect — arrays store collections, not the LCV.

answer.text: It must always be an int.

feedback.text: No — the LCV can be any type (e.g., sentinel values).

questiontext.text: Which description best matches a sentinel-based loop?

answer.text: It stops when a special value is entered.

feedback.text: Correct — the sentinel marks “no more input”.

answer.text: It always repeats a fixed number of times.

feedback.text: No — that’s a counter-controlled loop.

answer.text: It requires at least one array.

feedback.text: No — sentinel loops don’t require arrays.

answer.text: It works only with negative numbers.

feedback.text: Incorrect — the sentinel can be any agreed value.

questiontext.text: When can a flag-based loop stop looping/searching?

answer.text: When the required property has been found.

feedback.text: Exactly — once the flag is raised, the hunt is over.

answer.text: When all array elements are printed.

feedback.text: No — printing is unrelated.

answer.text: Only when a sentinel is detected.

feedback.text: No — that’s a different loop pattern.

answer.text: When the LCV becomes zero.

feedback.text: No — flag loops don’t rely on decreasing counters.

questiontext.text: Which of the following is essential in a counter-controlled loop?

answer.text: A known number of iterations.

feedback.text: Correct — counters are for predictable repetition.

answer.text: A sentinel value.

feedback.text: No — that belongs to sentinel loops.

answer.text: A boolean flag.

feedback.text: No — flag-based loops use flags.

answer.text: A switch statement.

feedback.text: No — loops do not require switch statements.

questiontext.text: When is a switch statement most appropriate?

answer.text: When selecting from a small number of exact options.

feedback.text: Correct — menus are a classic example.

answer.text: When comparing ranges of values.

feedback.text: No — ranges suit if/else, not switch.

answer.text: When constructing arrays.

feedback.text: No — switches do not build arrays.

answer.text: When validating user input lengths.

feedback.text: No — validation logic doesn’t require switch.

questiontext.text: What happens if the default is missing in a switch statement?

answer.text: Nothing happens if none of the named values were used

feedback.text: Correct — Java uses the default option if no other branch was executed.

answer.text: The program crashes.

feedback.text: No — it continues, just without a default action.

answer.text: The switch repeats itself.

feedback.text: No — switches don’t loop.

answer.text: The default case runs automatically.

feedback.text: No — default isn’t forced.

questiontext.text: What structure is typically used to keep a menu repeating?

answer.text: A loop controlled by the user’s menu option.

feedback.text: Correct — the LCV is usually the option variable.

answer.text: A switch inside another switch.

feedback.text: No — inception is not required.

answer.text: A recursive method.

feedback.text: No — recursion is excessive for menus.

answer.text: A boolean flag that never changes.

feedback.text: No — that loop would run forever.

questiontext.text: Why might arrays be used with sentinel loops?

answer.text: To store all valid inputs before the sentinel appears.

feedback.text: Correct — arrays keep the collected data.

answer.text: Because arrays generate sentinel values automatically.

feedback.text: No — arrays do not make magic numbers.

answer.text: To force the loop to run exactly 100 times.

feedback.text: No — sentinel loops do not force fixed iteration counts.

answer.text: Because arrays are required for switch statements.

feedback.text: Incorrect — switches don’t require arrays.

questiontext.text: What is the purpose of toString() in a class?

answer.text: To return a readable description of the object’s fields.

feedback.text: Correct — it formats the object into a user-friendly string.

answer.text: To print directly to the console.

feedback.text: No — printing is done outside toString().

answer.text: To validate fields.

feedback.text: No — validation is done in setters/constructors.

answer.text: To update numeric fields.

feedback.text: No — updating is done in setters.

questiontext.text: Which productCode value should be REJECTED according to the validation rules that productCode should be in the range 1000 - 9999 inclusive?

feedback.text: Correct — 10000 is outside the upper boundary.
No — 1000 is the lower valid boundary.
No — 2000 is well within range.
No — 9999 is the upper valid boundary.

questiontext.text: Which data types can a Java switch statement operate on?

answer.text: int, char, and String

feedback.text: Correct — these are supported types.

answer.text: double only

feedback.text: No — double cannot be switched on.

answer.text: boolean only

feedback.text: No — boolean is not permitted in switch.

answer.text: Arrays only

feedback.text: No — arrays cannot be used in switch.
